History and Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
31-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presents via telephone with a first-episode left-sided throbbing headache of 24-hour duration, accompanied by photophobia and no focal neurologic or infective features; clinical impression is new-onset migraine, with advice to add NSAID therapy, maintain hydration, and seek review if red-flag symptoms occur.

History:
• Presenting complaint – “Really bad” headache for ~1 day.  
• Onset – Began on waking the morning before consultation.  
• Character – Throbbing, moderate–severe, left-sided.  
• Course – Continuous baseline with fluctuating intensity; has not fully resolved.  
• Exacerbating factors – Bright light/sunlight.  
• Relieving factors – Lying down; dark room; paracetamol provides partial relief.  
• Associated symptoms – Photophobia.  
• Denied symptoms – Visual disturbance, aura, abnormal smells/tastes, nausea, vomiting, fever, rhinorrhoea, otalgia, rash, neck stiffness, weakness, numbness, tingling, positional or Valsalva worsening, skin changes.  
• Prior episodes – None; first headache of this type.  
• Menstrual relationship – None apparent; last period ~1 week ago.  
• Stress – Reports recent work-related stress.

Review of systems (only items specifically addressed):  
  – General: No fever, eating/drinking normally.  
  – Neurologic: No focal deficits, no sensory changes.  
  – HEENT: No visual changes, no sinus symptoms.  
  – Dermatologic: No rash.  

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses, surgeries, or hospitalizations reported.

Medications:
• Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive), dose/route/frequency not documented, started ~6 years ago.  
• Paracetamol for current pain, dose/route/frequency not documented.  

Allergies:
• Aspirin – causes marked nausea.

Social History:
• Lives with friends/housemates at 5 Kings Place (full address on registration).  
• Alcohol – “A few drinks at the weekend” (moderate).  
• Tobacco – Never smoker.  
• Recreational drugs – Denies use.  
• Occupation/stress – Work-related stress noted; details not given.

Family History:
• Mother – Hypertension and migraine.  
• No other familial conditions discussed.

Physical Examination:
(Telephone consultation – no in-person exam)  
• Vitals: Not measured; patient does not feel febrile.  
• Neurologic, HEENT, skin: No abnormalities elicited by history; no objective exam performed.

Investigations:
• None performed or available.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: New-onset unilateral throbbing headache – likely migraine without aura.  
  • Plan:  
    – Start NSAID (e.g., ibuprofen) in addition to ongoing paracetamol if no contraindication.  
    – Ensure adequate oral hydration, rest in dark room as needed.  
    – Monitor symptom course; if headache worsens, lasts >72 h, or develops new features (fever, rash, neck stiffness, visual change, focal neurology) to seek immediate medical review or emergency care.  
    – Consider headache diary and follow-up consultation if recurrent, menstrual-linked, or persistent to evaluate need for preventive therapy.

Issue 2: Blood pressure and general health screening.  
  • Plan:  
    – Arrange blood pressure check (patient last measured ~6 months ago).  
    – Advise purchase of home thermometer for monitoring fever should symptoms evolve.

Issue 3: Combined oral contraceptive use and thrombotic risk.  
  • Plan:  
    – No change at present; counsel that persistent/worsening headache despite simple analgesia warrants reassessment to exclude secondary causes such as cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.  
    – Reinforce avoidance of smoking and maintenance of healthy lifestyle to reduce vascular risk.

General advice:  
  • Re-contact clinic promptly for any red-flag symptoms (sudden “worst ever” headache, neurological deficit, vomiting, confusion, rash, persistent fever).  
  • Reassurance provided; patient voiced understanding and had no further questions.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Migraine without aura – High likelihood. Classic unilateral throbbing pain, photophobia, female with positive family history; absence of red-flag signs.  
2. Tension-type/stress-related headache – Moderate likelihood. Recent stress and fluctuating pain, but photophobia and throbbing quality less typical.  
3. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Low-moderate likelihood. Risk factor (combined OCP) and new headache; no focal neuro signs yet but warrants caution.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected elements: Objective vitals, neurological and fundoscopic exam, complete medication list with doses, comprehensive allergy review (other agents, reaction types), occupation/stress detail.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; minor inaudible segments did not obscure clinical content.
